## Órgiva, the balcony of 400 mm: transition and dryland crops

At an altitude of 450 meters, Órgiva marks the exact point where the Alpujarra leaves behind the direct influence of the Mediterranean and enters the climatic logic of the mountains. The 400 millimeters of annual rainfall recorded by its weather station exceed the figures for Motril, located just twenty kilometers further south, by a third. That difference of 100 millimeters is not just a simple statistical datum: it represents the invisible boundary between two agricultural worlds, two landscapes, and two ways of understanding water.

The Órgiva station, integrated into the Agricultural Information Network of the Junta de Andalucía, has been recording the vital signs of this transition territory for decades. Its historical series reveal an increase of 1.2 degrees Celsius since 1980, a figure that the ministry's technicians consider especially significant because it is an area where dryland crops depend on very precise thermal balances. The thermometer does not just measure heat: it measures the viability of an agricultural model that has worked for centuries.

In the fields surrounding the municipality, olive and almond trees share terraces with orange trees, a coexistence that surprises those who associate citrus fruits exclusively with coastal plains. The orange trees of Órgiva take advantage of the residual moisture that rises through the Guadalfeo valley and the still mild temperatures at this intermediate altitude. The olive trees, for their part, cling to the drier, stonier slopes, where no other species would compete for such ungrateful soil.

Local farmers have noticed changes that do not appear in official bulletins but that condition every campaign. The almond tree now blooms fifteen days earlier than in the 1990s, a phenological advance that the most veteran farmers describe with a mixture of astonishment and concern. This early flowering exposes the crops to late frosts that can still descend from Sierra Nevada in March, when the trees have already committed their annual production.

The risk is not theoretical. A frost during full bloom can reduce the almond harvest to zero in a matter of hours, and the farmers of Órgiva know this because they have lived it. The new generations consult weather apps on their mobile phones, but the final decision still depends on the reading of the sky their grandparents used to make. Technology has reached the terraces, although it has not entirely replaced memory.

The climatic transition represented by Órgiva is also manifested in the spontaneous vegetation. Prickly pears and agaves, typical of the coastal strip, begin to become scarce at this altitude, while the first chestnut trees appear in the cooler shaded areas. The landscape becomes greener and more compact, less mineral than that of the coast, but still far from the lushness that characterizes the high villages of the region.

The urban center of Órgiva, with its Renaissance church and its streets laid out in Moorish style, serves as the administrative capital of the lower Alpujarra. Its weekly market attracts farmers from all the nearby towns, who come down with their products and go back up with news, tools, and supplies. At the stalls, conversations can be heard about the price of almonds, the lack of rain, or the arrival of new foreign residents who have bought abandoned estates.

This mix of population has introduced experimental crops that coexist with the traditional ones. Small plantations of avocado and mango, unthinkable thirty years ago, now appear in the most sheltered areas of the municipal district. Technicians from the Agricultural Information Network follow these trials with interest, aware that climate change is pushing the boundary of subtropical crops upwards.

The data from the Órgiva station confirm this trend. Winter minimum temperatures have risen enough for cold-sensitive species to find viable conditions where they previously had none. However, water remains the limiting factor: the 400 millimeters of annual rainfall are not enough for irrigation-demanding crops, and the water concessions in the Guadalfeo basin are already fully committed.

The almond tree, the emblematic crop of this altitudinal band, exemplifies the paradox of climate change in dryland agriculture. On the one hand, the advance in flowering indicates that winters are milder and that the accumulation of winter chill is decreasing. On the other hand, this very mildness increases vulnerability to extreme events that have not disappeared, but have become more unpredictable.

The olive growers of Órgiva observe their trees with the patience of those who work with long cycles. An olive tree planted today will yield full harvests in twenty years, when climatic conditions will be different from those of today. This long-term uncertainty complicates investment decisions and pushes many owners to diversify, planting varieties more resistant to drought or combining olive groves with other uses.

The Órgiva weather station, with its sensors and automatic records, has become a reference point for scholars of the Andalusian climate. The 1.2-degree increase since 1980 places this municipality at the average of the warming recorded in the interior of the province of Granada, but with a particularity: here the change is observed directly on the ground, in the phenology of the crops and in the composition of the agricultural landscape.

The terraces surrounding the village, built centuries ago with dry stone, continue to fulfill their function of retaining soil and moisture. This traditional infrastructure, which does not appear in budgets or statistics, constitutes one of the best defenses against erosion and the irregularity of rainfall. The stone walls act like sponges that slow down runoff and allow water to infiltrate slowly.

Órgiva summarizes, in its 400 millimeters of rain and its 450 meters of altitude, the essence of the Alpujarra as a transition territory. Neither coast nor high mountain, this balcony over the Guadalfeo valley condenses the climatic tensions that define the present and condition the future of the region. The data from the weather station and the experience of the farmers tell the same story in different languages: the climate is changing, and the Alpujarra notices it before other places.
